Really cool take on the incremental genre. Had fun while playing and was nice to try and figure out how to proceed in some places. Idea felt like it was inspired by other incremental games and id like to believe its inspired by Undertale's combat mechanics, as it fuses the gameplay with incremental genre really well.

But as this is a review, i'll talk about several things that i think can be improved.

There are some pacing issues and i think it stems from the fact its hard to judge how long into the game a normal player 
can go with the upgrades they have, and thats totally understandable. I will list some issues and potential fixes i could think of while playing. 
- There is currently no way of generating enough red resource to upgrade everything if you are not constantly grinding 3-4 minute runs. I think the fact the All multiplier is stuck on top left where it requires 150k red resource to get to, is amplifying the issue even more. I have finished the game several times now and i still dont have enough to upgrade and unlock top left. As a completionist i will keep grinding, but moving it to another space or adding other ways for resource gain multiplier would be great - more on this later.
- I think the game should unlock a kind of unlimited mode, i couldnt find it even if exists. Red resource is increased exponentially as the game progresses but as you are stuck at a 5 minute timer there's no way to increase it further with time, your only way to amplify your gain is through upgrades, which are stuck behind more red resource required upgrades.
- Challenges section was underwhelming. As someone who loves incremental games that get amplified by the challenge times like Antimatter Dimensions, I thought challenges would be a lot more and work differently.
I think challenges could be reworked into something that has unique changes to how game functions. Like changing every resource with the blue one, always having the special event in the end of the game but a harder version etc.  And they would make more sense and would help a lot more if they were multipliers on the resource gen, while also having something like "All resource gain is multiplied by the average of your challenge completions" to push player more into challenges.
- Last power should have some kind of indicator for charge time. And it should charge even if you click and let go. I think i bugged it and wasted several uses because I couldnt hear the sound of it.
- And lastly, i really think it should include some kind of credits roll at the end for the first playthrough. And maybe remove the cutscene for the next ones, it takes too much time to watch while grinding for all upgrades

Aside from all these nitpicky points, i really love the game and wish it extended more because of how much i liked it. Looking forward to other games and potentially patches for the game from the dev. Really great job.

Minutescape is a Short and Sweet active incremental game, similar to others in its genre like Nodebuster or To The Core. I was definitely excited for this one as soon as I saw the demo earlier this year. Was the wait worth it? ... probably yea. 
You can expect about 3 hours of gameplay out of this one, probably some more if you want to challenge yourself but there's really not much reason to keep playing after you win. 

Like with most of these short incremental games you can probably expect to get some replay value in about a year or two after you first play depending on your personality.

The game is definitely not perfect and still has some things that probably need to be ironed out eventually. Here is what I thought from my experience playing it on launch day.

The main flaw the game has is its ability system. In the game there are four different abilities and you are allowed to bring any two of them with you to use in the "simulation". However, this is only half true in practice. The game pretty much forces you to use the third ability "Shield" which means you really only have one spare ability slot that the other three abilities have to compete for. Of the other three, "Shrink" is just generally superior to "Slow Time" in both cost and effect, and the final ability "Shockwave" is just completely awful and too expensive to upgrade.

I am not sure if this would negatively impact the game or not, but "Slow Time" really should have been the first ability that you unlock, instead of "Shrink"

The pacing also isn't anything you will really be writing home about. I wouldn't say that it is terrible, but I never felt anything particularly special about it. It does kind of end up gimping the final ability, and a few of the final economy upgrades are also super overpriced and will never be bought even by people who are bad at the game. A currency converter would have also been appreciated, as one of the five currencies runs out of things to buy significantly faster than the others.

It also wouldn't hurt to show the player that certain upgrades are still hiding more upgrades behind them. This is especially bad for upgrades related to the Shield ability, which is hidden behind not one but TWO levels of Slow Time upgrades. In my run I saw the writing on the wall for Slow Time and didn't bother investing in it, only finding out about my mistake later when [spoiler]I realized I had skipped an entire currency tier by accident [/spoiler]

The game is also quite linear, although that is not necessarily a bad thing for all people but it should still be noted for those who do care about it. Certain upgrades are also a bit ambiguous on what they actually do to help you "Fewer easy bullets as new appear" in particular sounds very strange.

Lastly, the ending of the game could use a little bit of work too. While incremental games aren't necessarily known for their endings the end to this one felt a little abrupt and flat. This game certainly has its own kind of charm and personality and it was a bit of a shame to not see that fully realized in the ending.

Conventional gamer wisdom says that 3 hours of gameplay for 6 dollars isn't offering you great bang for your buck, and looking at it through that lens there are undoubtedly many other, better games to spend your money on. Looking at it through the lens of an idle/incremental enjoyer though, this one certainly isn't too bad and can scratch the itch if you haven't played one in a while. It's not like 6 dollars an end of the world pricepoint or anything. If you like idle/incremental games you will probably end up playing this one eventually, although I would put it fairly low on the priority list unless you are looking for something really fast.

I haven't finished this game yet, but I have thoroughly enjoyed it. The mechanics are innovative, with soft restrictions on the game stages where it's not locked but pretty much impossible to reach the next stage without the relevant upgrades, which is also balanced well. The skill building of the player to go from dodging linear bullets to attracting resources to homing projectiles has a great, subtle learning curve, and the strategic element of exploration and safety doesn't press as hard as a lot of other games with the overwhelming amount of information and immediate strategy to learn.

A small sidenote is that I see limited customization, especially no option of choosing keybind for the ability keys. I do agree that dragging the mouse allows freer control on the character's hitbox than the 8 8-direction WASD control used in most other games, and how setting the ability keys to the mouse keys would make sense, but this is not friendly for touchpad players since it's difficult to press and move and also just to use both abilities. I would recommend either establishing alternative keybinds for the abilities or allowing the player to choose the keybinds for those.

I saw complaints that the game gets overly grindy during the two minute mark in game however this was not my experience, of course the game has grinding it is an incremental type game. However it's simply a standard snowballing chain that eventually sees you break through into the next resource of the game allowing for the building to repeat. Besides there's a pretty high skill ceiling that I found very satisfying to do good in once learned with abilities to boost your survivability and further increase it. Problems of repetition are doubtful in my opinion because there are many break points in the game that prevent this such as the introduction of challenges, trading and as mentioned prior abilities. Trading needs to be in more games because I can not emphasise enough how grateful I am for this mechanic as it saves the incredible tedium of grinding for a certain resource while having millions of higher value ones you wish you could swap for. Challenges also present a multiplicative buff towards certain attributes like speed, health and ability use cap making it very worth it to at least try the challenges. If you don't like what you see in the trailer you won't get it where as people that did I imagine would and end up, for the most part, enjoying this type of gameplay. All in all I enjoyed my time with the game but I would say to the developers please in future get better music I understand what you were going for given the games ending but please understand I think most like me would find it boring and draining on the ears, I just played my own music over it the whole time, you can do eerie music but it didn't fit the kind of theme the gameplay sets so despite the story it felt out of place and more annoying than anything. Speaking of sound design though would it be too much to ask for at least some effects on the projectiles making them more memorable or maybe when purchasing upgrades. But that's as far as my criticism goes for the game, given its price point and game time I think it's worth a buy

To be honest, I considered to give this game a thumbs-down. But since I got 3h out of the game (before I decided to quit playing because it became too frustrating) and I learned a lot from it, so I won't rate it negatively.

But from the three active incremental games I played recently (Nodebuster, Digseum, Minutescape), Minutescape is the weakest among them by far (and I loved Nodebuster and Digseum). In my opinion it has flaws in how the core loop and upgrading is designed to work together, and the upgrade-tree is unsatisfying to use and confusing at times. 50% of the research (2/4) is useless for my playstyle and skill, and not seeing what I'm researching beforehand is bad.
Ultimately I reached a point in where progress stalled and I could not upgrade anything meaningfully without playing the same thing over and over without anything changing. Maybe it's just that I made bad decisions in the upgrade tree, but I kind of doubt it, as I have almost everything unlocked except the things at the edge. So maybe it's only skill issue. I prefer these games to be more chill and relaxing, as were Nodebuster and Digseum. This here, in contrast, was more stressful and frustrating to me.

Minutescape is a deceptively simple game that manages to deliver a deeply engaging, reflex-driven experience by stripping gameplay down to its bare essentials. You don’t shoot, attack, or build anything—instead, you survive. That’s it. The entire objective is to last five minutes inside a constantly shifting bullet hell arena where projectiles, enemies, and hazards come at you from every angle. You control a small shape, dodging with precision as the intensity ramps up over time. This core mechanic—minimalist as it may be—quickly reveals a surprising amount of depth and tension. It’s one of those rare games where doing less makes you feel more.

What elevates Minutescape beyond a basic arcade dodger is its synergy between real-time skill and long-term progression. Every run earns you currency that feeds into an extensive upgrade system, allowing you to slowly mold your avatar into a more survivable force. Speed boosts, hitbox reduction, temporary shields, and time-slowing abilities all become tools in your kit, and choosing how to allocate your points becomes a compelling part of the experience. The more you invest, the more dynamic your runs become, as you test new combinations and slowly work your way toward the elusive five-minute survival goal. It’s a clever feedback loop that encourages both experimentation and mechanical improvement—your reflexes matter just as much as your build.

Each run begins with a calm sense of possibility, but that peace doesn't last long. The arena becomes progressively more claustrophobic as new projectile types are introduced. First come the simple red bullets; then chasers, laser walls, rotating patterns, and even shrinking safe zones start forcing you into tighter movement spaces. The escalation feels carefully calibrated. At around 90 seconds, the difficulty curve jumps significantly, and if you haven’t upgraded wisely or mastered evasive techniques, your run ends fast. This pressure creates an addictive tension—the “just one more try” sensation that defines a good roguelite. You’re constantly learning, not only how to react but how to prepare.

Visually, the game keeps everything clean and focused. The color palette is muted but distinct, which helps readability in a chaotic environment. Projectiles and hazards are clearly telegraphed, and the UI remains unobtrusive, letting you keep your attention on survival. The minimalist aesthetic may not stand out in screenshots, but it’s extremely functional and contributes to the tight, focused feel of the game. Sound design is similarly streamlined—audio cues are subtle but useful, and the music loops help keep you in a state of concentration without becoming distracting or repetitive.

Despite its low cost and small file size, Minutescape feels polished and thoughtfully designed. It supports keyboard, mouse, and full controller input, and it's accessible across platforms with strong performance even on low-end machines. The game has benefitted from its developer's responsiveness to player feedback during early access and demo phases. Features like customizable controls, visual tweaks, and balance adjustments were added based on real-time community input, which gives the game a more refined feel than many small indie titles in the same space.

Player feedback has been mostly positive, with many praising the game’s pure focus and satisfying difficulty. The Steam reviews highlight the game’s tight controls, the addictiveness of the five-minute loop, and the sense of accomplishment that comes from squeezing through the chaos with only seconds remaining. However, some criticisms do emerge—chiefly that early progression can feel slow, especially before key upgrades unlock the more interesting abilities. Others note that the gameplay loop, while well-executed, can start to feel repetitive over time, especially for players seeking a broader variety of modes, enemies, or mechanics.

Still, these issues don’t detract much from what Minutescape sets out to be. It’s not pretending to be a sprawling adventure or a feature-packed sandbox. It’s a game about movement, reaction, and resilience. Every second survived is earned, and every failure teaches you something. It’s challenging without being punishing, fast-paced without being overwhelming, and minimalist without being empty. For players who enjoy distilled arcade experiences, where your success hinges entirely on focus and timing, this is a compelling and affordable option.

Ultimately, Minutescape thrives by knowing exactly what it is and committing fully to that vision. It doesn't waste your time with fluff or filler—it gives you a simple task and dares you to get good at it. As you inch closer to the five-minute mark, with projectiles closing in from every direction and your screen pulsing with tension, you start to realize how much can be done with so little. It's a stripped-down, high-intensity survival challenge that demands attention and rewards persistence. And for players who enjoy that kind of test, Minutescape more than earns its place in the bullet hell roguelite pantheon.

Minutescape brings a refreshing element of precision and skill into the incremental game genre. The game loop centers around going in and out of a "simulation", with breaks in between to upgrade abilities and attributes for your character. What separates this game from others in the genre is that the player has as much room to improve at the action portion of the game as the character does in the upgrade portion of the game. The gameplay's reliance on your reflexes and strategy is what keeps the experience fresh and rewarding.

The game is short, and depending on skill might take 3-9 hours to beat. Though there is an element of grind that can make the game feel like it's dragging at certain points in the progression, it is minimal and more engaging than the the grinding required for most incremental games.

One element that really hooked me was the vibe of the game - though it uses very limited storytelling devices, the look and feel, music, and text dialogue create an eerie, retro-dystopian feel, reminiscent to shows like "Black Mirror" and "Severance".

The low price is fair for the interesting concept and the 5-10 hours of engagement it offers if you opt to fully complete it.

The core of the game is pretty fun. Try to survive for awhile, get some currency, improve and unlock things. I suppose I did enjoy it and it's not too terrible for the price, but it left me with a bad taste in my mouth and feeling unsatisfied.

The problem is mainly in the meta-loop. It bills itself as an "unfolding game" but there isn't that much that unfolds. The vast majority of the upgrades are just incremental stat increases, and only a handful of things actually change how the game actually plays.

That alone wouldn't be too bad. But the problem is you have to do a lot of grinding to get enough of the currency to make progress. You'll end up doing 2-3 runs with out having actually purchased any substantive upgrades before you can afford anything. It took me about 6 hours to beat, but it felt like it should have been only half of that based on the amount of content. (The way progression is gated behind a few key purchases without being clear that it is gated by them also made it take a bit longer than it should).

Honestly, I suspect the dev was worried that people would refund if it was less than 2 hours, so padded out the play length but made the game worse overall. 

You also probably don't enter into a game like this expecting much in the way of plot, though with the way it presented the "manual" as part of the unfolding experience made it feel like it had a lot of potential. But in the end, the "plot" is just incredibly disappointing.
